title: Docker Networking & Volumes: The Field Handbook
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on how Docker containers talk to the network and how they keep data, covering network namespaces, bridge/host/none/overlay drivers, port publishing, DNS and service discovery, bind mounts vs named volumes, tmpfs, drivers, backup, and the UID/GID permission traps that break real deployments.

chapters.title: Why Containers Need Their Own Network & Storage
points: A container is a process on the host wrapped in namespaces + cgroups — not a VM; networking and storage isolation come from Linux kernel primitives, not virtual hardware.
Namespace types Docker uses: pid, mnt, net, uts, ipc, user, cgroup — `net` gives each container its own interfaces/routes/iptables, `mnt` gives it its own mount tree.
Two problems this creates: (1) the container's ports are unreachable from outside by default, (2) the container's filesystem dies with the container.
The union filesystem: image layers are read-only, plus one thin writable container layer on top (copy-on-write). Writes copy the whole file up into the writable layer first.
Why the writable layer is bad for data: it's slow for write-heavy workloads, tied to container lifetime, and not shareable between containers.
`docker run --rm` deletes the writable layer on exit; without `--rm` it lingers — `docker system df` shows how much space stopped containers hold.
Ephemeral vs durable: application code belongs in the image, configuration comes in at run time, state belongs in a volume.
The 12-factor rule of thumb: treat containers as disposable; if `docker rm` loses something important, it should have been a volume.
Quick demo: `docker run -it alpine ip addr` shows only `lo` and `eth0`, no host interfaces — proof of net namespace isolation.
Roadmap for the handbook: namespaces → bridge → ports → DNS → other drivers → volumes → permissions → debugging.

chapters.title: Network Namespaces & the veth Pair
points: A network namespace holds its own interfaces, IP addresses, routing table, ARP table, and netfilter/iptables rules.
A veth pair is a virtual ethernet cable: two ends, packets in one end come out the other. One end lives in the container (`eth0`), the other on the host (`vethXXXX`).
The host end of the veth is enslaved to a Linux bridge (`docker0` for the default bridge network).
Inspect it: `ip link` on the host shows `vethXXXX@ifN`; `docker exec c ip link` shows `eth0@ifM` — the numbers cross-reference the two ends.
`docker network inspect bridge` lists connected containers with their IPs and MACs; `docker inspect -f '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}' c` gets one container's IP.
Loopback: every container gets its own `lo` at 127.0.0.1 — so `localhost` inside a container is the container, not the host. This is the #1 beginner confusion.
Enter a container's namespace from the host: `nsenter -t $(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' c) -n ip addr` — works even on images with no shell tools.
MTU inheritance: the veth/bridge MTU defaults to 1500; on VPN/overlay hosts with lower MTU this causes hangs on large payloads that ping doesn't reveal.
Container IPs are not stable — they are reassigned from the subnet pool on restart. Never hardcode them; use DNS names.
`--network=container:other` shares another container's namespace entirely (same IP, same ports) — the mechanism behind Kubernetes pods and sidecars.

chapters.title: The Bridge Driver: Default vs User-Defined
points: The default `bridge` network (`docker0`, usually 172.17.0.0/16) is what containers join when you pass no `--network`.
A user-defined bridge is created with `docker network create mynet` and joined with `--network mynet`.
Killer difference: user-defined bridges give automatic DNS resolution by container name; the default bridge does not (only the deprecated `--link` did).
Isolation: containers on different user-defined bridges cannot reach each other; every container on the default bridge can reach every other.
User-defined bridges support attach/detach on a running container: `docker network connect mynet c` / `docker network disconnect`.
A container can be on multiple networks at once — it gets one `eth0`, `eth1`, … per network, with its own IP on each. Common for a proxy that fronts an isolated backend.
Custom subnets: `docker network create --subnet 10.20.0.0/16 --gateway 10.20.0.1 mynet`, and static IPs with `--ip` at run time.
`--internal` creates a network with no outbound NAT — useful for a database tier that must never reach the internet.
ICC (inter-container communication) and `--icc=false` on the daemon block default-bridge traffic; user-defined networks are preferred over fiddling with this.
Compose creates a user-defined bridge per project automatically and names it `<project>_default` — services resolve each other by service name for free.
Address pool exhaustion: `could not find an available, non-overlapping IPv4 address pool` means too many networks; fix with `docker network prune` or `default-address-pools` in `daemon.json`.

chapters.title: Publishing Ports: -p, EXPOSE, and the NAT Path
points: `-p HOST:CONTAINER` publishes a port; `-p 8080:80` maps host 8080 to container 80. The order is host-first — reversing it is a classic bug.
`EXPOSE 80` in a Dockerfile is documentation plus a hint for `-P`; it publishes nothing on its own.
`-P` (capital) publishes every EXPOSEd port to a random high host port; `docker port c` reveals the assignments.
Bind address: `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` binds only to loopback so the service is not exposed on the host's public interface; bare `-p 8080:80` binds 0.0.0.0.
Protocol: `-p 53:53/udp` — TCP is the default, so UDP services need the suffix explicitly.
Ranges: `-p 8000-8010:8000-8010` maps a block in one flag.

Under the hood: Docker adds a DNAT rule in the iptables `nat` table (`DOCKER` chain) rewriting the destination to the container IP, plus a MASQUERADE rule for outbound. Inspect with `iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n`.
`docker-proxy` is a userland fallback process that handles cases iptables can't (e.g. host-local loopback hairpin); it's why you may see a process holding the port.

Docker's iptables rules are inserted ahead of most UFW/firewalld rules, so `-p 8080:80` can punch through a firewall you believed was closed. Bind to 127.0.0.1 or set `iptables: false` and manage rules yourself.
Outbound traffic needs no publishing at all — containers can reach the internet by default via NAT; publishing is only for inbound.
`Error starting userland proxy: bind: address already in use` means the host port is taken — find it with `ss -ltnp | grep 8080`.
You cannot publish a port on `--network host` (the flag is ignored with a warning) — the container already uses host ports directly.

chapters.title: Host, None, and the Other Network Drivers
points: `--network host`: no net namespace at all — the container shares the host's interfaces and port space. Fastest (no NAT, no veth hop) but zero isolation and port collisions are real.
Host mode on Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) does NOT mean your laptop's network — the Linux VM is the host; this trips people constantly.
`--network none`: a namespace with only `lo`. Use for batch jobs that must have no connectivity, or when you'll wire up networking yourself.

`macvlan`: gives the container its own MAC and an IP on the physical LAN — it appears as a separate machine to the rest of the network. Needs promiscuous mode; host-to-container traffic is blocked by design.
`ipvlan`: same idea but shares the host MAC (L2 or L3 mode) — for networks/clouds that reject multiple MACs per port.
`overlay`: VXLAN-based multi-host networking for Swarm services; encapsulates container traffic between nodes. `--attachable` lets standalone containers join.
Comparison row — bridge: NAT, isolated, DNS by name, needs `-p`. host: no NAT, no isolation, no `-p`, best latency. none: nothing. macvlan: LAN-native IP, no NAT, no port publishing needed.
Reaching the host from a container: `host.docker.internal` on Desktop; on Linux add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` or use the bridge gateway IP.
`docker network ls` shows drivers and scope (local vs swarm); the three built-ins `bridge`, `host`, `none` cannot be removed.
Choosing: default to a user-defined bridge; reach for host only for measured performance needs or high-port-count services; macvlan when the container must be a first-class LAN citizen.

chapters.title: Embedded DNS & Service Discovery
points: Docker runs an embedded DNS resolver at 127.0.0.11 inside every container on a user-defined network; `/etc/resolv.conf` inside the container points at it.
Names resolved: container name, hostname (`--hostname`), and network aliases (`--network-alias`). Compose adds the service name.
Unmatched queries are forwarded to the daemon's upstream resolvers (host `/etc/resolv.conf`, or `--dns` flags / `daemon.json` `dns` setting).
Multiple containers sharing one network alias produce multiple A records — a crude round-robin load balance, but clients cache DNS, so it's not a real balancer.
Compose scaling: `docker compose up --scale web=3` — resolving `web` returns all three IPs.
DNS is per-network: a container on two networks resolves names from both; a container on the default bridge resolves none of its peers.
Debug: `docker exec c getent hosts other` or `nslookup other`; `cat /etc/resolv.conf` to confirm 127.0.0.11 is present.
Alpine/musl caveat: musl libc queries all nameservers in parallel and has historically mishandled some responses — a source of flaky DNS on Alpine images.
`--link` is legacy: it injected `/etc/hosts` entries and env vars, is one-directional, doesn't survive restarts cleanly. Deprecated — use user-defined networks.
Real-world pattern: app connects to `postgres:5432` by service name; no IPs, no ports published, database stays unreachable from the host.

chapters.title: Volumes vs Bind Mounts vs tmpfs
points: Three mount types: named volume (Docker-managed dir under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/`), bind mount (any host path), tmpfs (RAM only, never written to disk).
Named volume syntax: `-v myvol:/data` or `--mount type=volume,src=myvol,dst=/data`. Docker creates the volume if it doesn't exist.
Bind mount syntax: `-v /host/path:/container/path` or `--mount type=bind,src=/host/path,dst=/container/path`. The host path must be absolute — a relative path is parsed as a volume name.
tmpfs: `--tmpfs /tmp` or `--mount type=tmpfs,dst=/tmp,tmpfs-size=64m` — fast, wiped on stop, good for secrets and scratch files.

`-v` vs `--mount`: `-v` is terse and auto-creates missing host paths (as root-owned dirs — a common surprise); `--mount` is explicit, key=value, and errors if the source is missing. Prefer `--mount` in scripts.

Volume initialization: when an empty named volume is mounted onto a path that has content in the image, the image content is copied into the volume. Bind mounts never do this — they shadow whatever was there.
That copy happens only once, when the volume is empty — a stale volume keeps old content even after you rebuild the image. Classic 'my code changes don't appear' bug.
Read-only mounts: `-v myvol:/data:ro` or `--mount ...,readonly` — pair with `--read-only` on the container for a hardened rootfs plus writable tmpfs.
Anonymous volumes: `-v /data` with no name creates a random-hashed volume; Dockerfile `VOLUME /data` does the same on every run and quietly accumulates garbage.

Comparison row — portability: volumes win (no host path dependency). Live editing: bind mounts win (dev workflows). Performance on Linux: about equal. On Desktop macOS/Windows: bind mounts are much slower (filesystem sharing over a VM boundary).
Decision rule: bind mount for source code in development and for host config files; named volume for databases and anything production; tmpfs for secrets and scratch.

chapters.title: Named Volumes: Lifecycle, Drivers, and Sharing
points: CLI surface: `docker volume create`, `ls`, `inspect`, `rm`, `prune`. `inspect` shows `Mountpoint` — the real host path under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data`.
Volumes outlive containers by design. `docker rm c` keeps the volume; `docker rm -v c` also removes that container's ANONYMOUS volumes (not named ones).

`docker volume prune` deletes volumes not referenced by any container — including stopped containers' volumes only if the container is gone. Destructive: verify with `docker volume ls -f dangling=true` first.
Compose named volumes are prefixed with the project name; `docker compose down` keeps them, `docker compose down -v` deletes them.

Sharing one volume across containers is fine and common — e.g. an app writes uploads, a backup sidecar reads them. Concurrent writers need application-level coordination; the filesystem gives you no locking guarantees across containers.
`--volumes-from other` inherits all of another container's mounts — the classic 'data container' pattern, now largely superseded by named volumes.

Volume drivers: `local` is default; plugins provide NFS, CIFS/SMB, cloud block storage. Example NFS volume: `docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw --opt device=:/exports/data nfsvol`.
Labels for housekeeping: `docker volume create --label project=app data` then `docker volume ls -f label=project=app`.
Backup idiom: `docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/vol.tgz -C /data .`; restore by reversing the tar into a fresh volume.
Never `cp` into `/var/lib/docker/volumes/` on a live system as your normal workflow — it works on the local driver but breaks with other drivers and bypasses Docker's bookkeeping.
Databases specifically: mount the data dir (`/var/lib/postgresql/data`, `/var/lib/mysql`) as a named volume, never a Desktop bind mount — the shared filesystem can break fsync/locking semantics.

chapters.title: The Permissions Problem: UID, GID, and Ownership
points: Mounts carry numeric UID/GID, not usernames. The kernel checks numbers; the container's `/etc/passwd` names are irrelevant to the host.
So UID 1000 inside the container is UID 1000 on the host — even if it's `appuser` in the container and `sathwik` on the host. Same number, different name, same permissions.
Symptom: `Permission denied` writing to a bind mount, because the host directory is owned by your user and the container process runs as root or a different UID.
Fix A — match the UID at run time: `docker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g) ...`. Downside: that UID may have no entry in the container's `/etc/passwd`, so `whoami` fails and `$HOME` is unset.
Fix B — build for it: `RUN adduser -u 1000 -D app` then `USER app` in the Dockerfile, and `chown` the app directories during build.
Fix C — chown the host directory to the container's UID: `sudo chown -R 1000:1000 ./data`.

Named volumes are gentler: on first use Docker copies the image's content AND its ownership into the empty volume, so an image that ships a correctly-owned dir just works. Bind mounts get no such help.
`--user` cannot be changed after start, and setting it can break images whose entrypoint drops privileges itself (e.g. official Postgres expects to start as root then `su-exec` to `postgres`).

Root-in-container ≠ root-on-host only if user namespace remapping (`userns-remap` in `daemon.json`) is on; by default container root IS host root on a bind-mounted file. This is a real privilege-escalation path.
Never bind-mount `/var/run/docker.sock` into an untrusted container — access to the daemon socket is equivalent to root on the host.
SELinux hosts (RHEL/Fedora): add `:z` (shared) or `:Z` (private) to the mount — `-v ./data:/data:Z` — or every access fails with `Permission denied` despite correct ownership.
Windows/Desktop: bind mounts go through a translation layer and report permissive modes (often 0777); permission bugs may only surface once you deploy to Linux.

chapters.title: Compose: Networks and Volumes Declared
points: Compose creates one default bridge network per project; every service joins it and resolves peers by service name. No `links` needed.
Declare extra networks under a top-level `networks:` key and attach services with a per-service `networks:` list — the standard frontend/backend split.
`ports:` publishes to the host (`"8080:80"` — quote it, or YAML parses `5432:5432`-style values with a leading zero oddly); `expose:` only documents.
Top-level `volumes:` declares named volumes; `external: true` says 'this volume already exists, don't create or delete it'.
Service-level short syntax `./src:/app` is a bind mount; `appdata:/var/lib/data` (a name declared above) is a volume. Same string position, totally different semantics — read carefully.
Long syntax is explicit and preferred: `- type: bind, source: ./src, target: /app` with options like `read_only: true` and `consistency`.
`depends_on` waits for start, not readiness — pair it with a `healthcheck` and `condition: service_healthy` or the app will connect before the database is listening.
`network_mode: host` on a service disables Compose's networking for it and makes `ports:` meaningless.
Dev override pattern: base file mounts nothing, `docker-compose.override.yml` adds the source bind mount and hot reload — production runs the base file alone.
The anonymous-volume trick for node_modules: `- ./app:/app` plus `- /app/node_modules` keeps the container's installed modules from being shadowed by the host directory.
`docker compose down` removes containers and the project network but keeps named volumes; `-v` removes them; `--remove-orphans` cleans services deleted from the file.

chapters.title: Debugging Network & Mount Problems
points: Step 1, always: `docker inspect c` and read `.NetworkSettings` and `.Mounts` — the truth about what actually got wired, versus what you meant to wire.
`docker port c` confirms published ports; `ss -ltnp` on the host confirms something is listening on the host side.
'Connection refused' from the host usually means the app inside is bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 — inside the container, loopback is unreachable from outside. Bind to 0.0.0.0.
'Connection refused' between containers usually means they're not on the same user-defined network, or you used the host-published port instead of the container's real port.
Timeouts (rather than refusals) point at firewall, routing, or MTU — refusals mean the packet arrived and nothing was listening.
Toolbox trick for scratch/distroless images: `docker run --rm -it --network container:target nicolaka/netshoot` gives you `dig`, `tcpdump`, `curl`, `ss` inside the target's namespace.
Capture traffic from the host: `tcpdump -i docker0` or `-i vethXXXX` to see exactly what crosses the bridge.
Mount debugging: `docker exec c ls -lan /path` — the `-n` prints numeric UID/GID, which is what actually matters for permissions.

'My file changes aren't showing': check whether the path is shadowed by another mount, whether the volume was pre-populated and is now stale, and whether the build COPYed the file into a different directory.
Disk pressure: `docker system df -v` breaks down images, containers, and volumes; dangling volumes are a frequent silent consumer of a full disk.
Reproduce minimally: two `alpine` containers on one network, `nc -l -p 8080` in one and `nc other 8080` in the other — proves the network path independently of your app.

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Performance, and Security Posture
points: Bridge networking costs a veth traversal plus iptables NAT per packet — measurable at high packet rates, invisible for typical web services.
Host networking removes both, cutting latency and CPU overhead; benchmark before adopting, because you pay with lost isolation and manual port management.
macvlan avoids NAT while keeping a separate namespace, but requires LAN cooperation (promiscuous mode, DHCP coordination) and blocks host-to-container traffic.
Overlay adds VXLAN encapsulation: ~50 bytes of header, lower effective MTU, and encryption cost if enabled — the price of multi-host.
Storage: on Linux, volumes and bind mounts both hit the host filesystem directly and perform the same; the container's writable layer is the slow one because of copy-on-write.
On Docker Desktop, bind mounts cross a VM boundary (virtiofs/gRPC-FUSE) — orders of magnitude slower for many small files. Named volumes stay inside the VM and are fast.
Security: publish narrowly (`-p 127.0.0.1:...`), put databases on `--internal` networks with no published ports, and let a reverse proxy be the only container with host ports.

Run as non-root (`USER` in the Dockerfile), add `--read-only` with tmpfs for writable paths, and drop capabilities (`--cap-drop=ALL`) — mount and network isolation is only as good as the process privileges.
Secrets do not belong in bind-mounted files with loose permissions or in env vars visible via `docker inspect`; use tmpfs mounts or a secrets manager.
Operational trade-off: named volumes are portable and safe but opaque (you can't easily browse them); bind mounts are transparent but tie the container to a host layout.
Rule of thumb for the whole topic: isolate by default, open one hole at a time, and know which of the three mount types you're using before you debug anything.

chapters.title: Summary: The Whole Model on One Page
points: Networking model: net namespace + veth pair + bridge + iptables NAT. Everything else is a variation on which of those pieces you skip.
Driver cheat sheet — bridge: default, isolated, NAT, DNS by name. host: shared stack, no NAT, no `-p`. none: isolated, no connectivity. macvlan/ipvlan: LAN-native IP. overlay: multi-host VXLAN.
Always use a user-defined bridge, never the default one — you get DNS by container name and real isolation for free.
Ports: `-p host:container`, host side first. `EXPOSE` publishes nothing. Bind to 127.0.0.1 unless you truly want the world.
Inside a container, `localhost` is that container. Bind services to 0.0.0.0; reach the host via `host.docker.internal` (add `--add-host=...:host-gateway` on Linux).

Storage cheat sheet — named volume: Docker-managed, portable, pre-populated from the image, the production default. Bind mount: host path, live editing, the dev default. tmpfs: RAM, secrets and scratch.
The volume-init rule: an empty volume is seeded from the image (content and ownership) exactly once; a stale volume silently keeps old data.
Permissions are numeric. Match UIDs (`--user`, `USER`, `chown`), remember container root is host root on a bind mount, and add `:Z` on SELinux hosts.
Lifecycle: `docker rm -v` drops anonymous volumes only; `compose down -v` drops project volumes; `volume prune` drops everything unreferenced — all three are easy to run by accident.
Debug order: `docker inspect` → is it listening on 0.0.0.0 → same network? → firewall/MTU → `netshoot` in the target's namespace.
Final mental model: the image is the code, the network is the wiring, the volume is the state. Keep the three separate and containers stay disposable.
